steps.drill: Box breathing 4-4-4-4, then wall push isometric 'release the brake'
steps.dose: 3 breath cycles, then 2 × 6 s max-intent wall push in an athletic split stance
steps.why: The slow exhale downshifts the threat state that makes you freeze then react late. The 6 s max push tells the nervous system that high force is safe, so more fast-twitch units come online for the first sprint.

steps.dose: 20 s near-far (thumb → rim), then 10 tosses of the ball toward your face that you catch at chest
steps.why: Eyes are the first link in the chain. A ball coming straight at you is the threat cue; catching 10 easy ones teaches the brain it's safe, so it stops flinching and grabbing on passes.

steps.drill: The Screw into ready position + pogos
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw holds (feet planted, rotate outward into the floor), then 2 × 15 pogos
steps.why: Flat feet let the arch collapse, ankle roll in and knee cave. The Screw torques the arch up and fires glutes; pogos then stiffen the Achilles spring so the first step bounces instead of sinks.

steps.dose: 6 closeouts (sprint 3 steps, chop, land and freeze 1 s in ready position: knees ~25°, hips hinged ~15°), 2 × 4 slides each way
steps.why: Freezing 1 s on every landing burns a balanced stop into the motor map, so you stop reaching and lunging and your feet are under you on defense without thinking.

steps.dose: 10 one-hand shots from 3 ft, then 10 from the elbow: legs push, ball leaves at the top
steps.why: Your sequencing fires arm-first. Close shots where the legs clearly start the motion re-order the chain: ground → hips → shoulder → wrist, so the release is the last link of the whip.

steps.dose: 3 × baseline-to-half-court at 60/80/95%, then 3 two-foot rebound jumps touching as high as possible
steps.why: Ramping intensity gives a variable-intensity warm-up (airways) and recruits high-threshold motor units so the first possession isn't your slowest.

anchorCue: Between possessions: two quick bounces, land in ready.
airwayNote: Basketball is stop-start high intensity, a classic EIB trigger. The build-up sprints double as a variable-intensity warm-up, which reduced the post-exercise lung-function drop in a systematic review (Stickland 2012, grade B); protection lasts roughly 1-2 h for many people (some see up to ~2-4 h). Keep sprints short: aim for HR ~170-185 (≈85-90% of max ~200-205) for brief bursts, then walk. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Long static stretches (>30 s per muscle) right before playing
Heavy lifting or max-rep jumps before the game
Thinking about form during play: the patterns are installed now
teachMe: Speed on the court is mostly perception plus a stiff, well-aligned base. Your eyes set how early you can act and your feet set how fast you can push. This protocol primes both: it calms the threat response so vision opens up, then lines up the foot-knee-hip stack so ground reaction force goes straight up the chain instead of leaking through a collapsed arch.

steps.dose: 3 slow breaths (4 s in nose, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: A long exhale turns off the gripping, protective tension that makes swings stiff. The isometric primes maximal recruitment without fatigue.

steps.dose: 20 s fast eye jumps between two targets ~1 m apart, then 10 underhand tosses toward your face from a partner/wall that you track to the glove
steps.why: Hitting and fielding fail on the eyes first. Tracking an approaching ball all the way in teaches the brain the ball is safe, which kills the flinch that makes contact random.

steps.drill: The Screw in batting stance + tripod rock
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw holds in stance, 5 slow rocks onto back-leg tripod (big toe, pinky toe, heel)
steps.why: A flat back foot rolls in and dumps the load before the swing starts. Screwing the feet into the ground loads the back hip so rotation can start from the floor.

steps.dose: 8 Hip Snaps (bat across shoulders, load back hip, snap hips to face the pitcher, hands stay back), then 8 dry swings at 70%
steps.why: Your arm fires first and the body catches up late. Hip Snaps with the hands locked force the order ground → hips → trunk → arms, so the bat becomes the last, fastest link of the whip.

steps.dose: 3 dry swings each at low / middle / high contact, then 6 ground-ball shuffles to the side, stick 1 s, throw
steps.why: Swinging through three reference heights calibrates bat path, so you're not guessing. Sticking the field-and-set position teaches feet-before-arm on the throw.

steps.dose: 10 throws building 50 → 90% distance, then 2 × 20 m sprints at 80/95%
steps.why: Arm tissues and the shoulder need graded load before max throws, and short sprints wake up the fast-twitch fibers for base running.

anchorCue: Between pitches: feel both feet screw into the dirt.
avoid: Max-effort throws or swings in the first minute
Long static stretching of the shoulder or hamstrings right before
Weighted-bat donut swings as a warm-up: they temporarily distort bat-speed feel
teachMe: A swing is a ground-to-bat energy transfer. Each link (feet, hips, trunk, arms) speeds up and then brakes so the next link goes faster, like cracking a whip. If the arm leads, the big engines (legs, hips) never get to contribute and contact is random. You're installing the order now so the game doesn't need you to think.

steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push from a 3-point-style lean
steps.why: Down-regulates the threat state so you read plays instead of freezing. The lean isometric rehearses the exact body angle of a drive.

steps.dose: 10 tosses toward your face caught at chest, then 6 catches where you stare at a fixed point and catch a ball tossed from the side
steps.why: Catching starts with letting the ball come to you without a flinch. Peripheral catches train the wide-field vision you use for reading defenders.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 15 pogos, 2 × 10 m A-skips
steps.why: Your arch collapses under load. The Screw sets a stiff tripod and the pogos stiffen the ankle spring, so the first step drives instead of sinking.

steps.dose: 6 cuts (3 each way): 5 m jog, plant, freeze 1 s with knee over the 2nd toe, go
steps.why: Freezing the plant installs knee-over-foot alignment, which counters valgus caused by flat feet and makes cuts sharper and safer.

steps.drill: Hip-led throws (if QB/throwing) or route stems
steps.dose: 8 throws at 60% stepping toward the target with hips opening first, or 4 routes at 70%
steps.why: Hips-then-arm sequencing adds distance with less arm stress; route stems groove deceleration mechanics before game speed.

steps.dose: 3 × 20 m at 70/85/95%, walk back
steps.why: Graded speed recruits high-threshold motor units and doubles as an interval-style warm-up for your airways.

anchorCue: In your stance: tripod feet, then go.
airwayNote: Repeated sprints are a common EIB trigger. Short build-up sprints act as an interval-style warm-up, which cut the post-exercise drop in lung function in a systematic review (Stickland 2012, grade B), with protection lasting roughly 1-2 h. Brief bursts to HR ~170-185, then walk. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Long static stretches before
Full-contact drills as a warm-up
New tackling technique on game day
teachMe: Acceleration is a force-angle problem: you need to push the ground backward and down while leaning forward, and a collapsing foot wastes that push sideways. Priming the foot and the eyes first means the push goes straight through the chain and the read happens earlier.

steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s nose in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Lowers threat arousal so your touch is soft, and recruits more muscle for the first sprint.

steps.dose: 20 s quick head-and-eye scans left-right, 20 s near-far (ball at feet → far goal)
steps.why: Good players scan before receiving. Fast eye shifts wake up the visual system so you see pressure early instead of reacting late.

steps.drill: The Screw + single-leg tripod balance + pogos
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 20 s per leg on tripod foot, 2 × 15 pogos
steps.why: Every pass and shot is on one leg. A stable tripod on the plant foot stops the ankle rolling in, so energy goes into the ball instead of into wobble.

steps.dose: 6 plant-and-freeze (1 s) cuts, then 20 one-touch wall passes alternating feet
steps.why: Freezing on the plant installs a balanced base; one-touch passes groove the plant-foot-next-to-ball pattern so touches stop being random.

steps.dose: 3 × 30 m at 60/80/95%, then 3 shots at 80% with hips leading the swing
steps.why: Graded intensity primes sprint speed and the hip-first striking chain, and protects the airways.

anchorCue: Before the ball comes: check your shoulder, then show your tripod.
airwayNote: Continuous running in cool air is a strong EIB trigger. The variable-intensity build-up runs are your airway warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Keep HR ~160-185 in short bursts, walk between. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Long static stretches before
Hard shooting before the legs are warm
Full-speed sprints in the first 2 minutes
teachMe: Soccer is a balance sport disguised as a running sport: the plant leg decides how cleanly force reaches the ball. Your flat feet make the plant leg wobble, so the drills set the arch and lock the knee over the foot before any ball work.

steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Calms the grip-everything threat response so strokes stay loose, and primes recruitment for the first explosive step.

steps.dose: 10 tossed balls tracked to the strings of a racket held still, then 20 s following a moving ball with eyes only
steps.why: Fear of the ball shows up as eyes leaving early. Watching easy balls all the way onto the strings teaches the brain the ball is safe.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 3 × 8 split-step pogos landing in ready (knees ~25°, hips ~15°)
steps.why: The split-step is an elastic pre-load. Stiff ankles plus an arched foot mean the push-off happens instantly instead of after a sag.

steps.dose: 8 Hip Snaps with racket across chest, then 8 shadow strokes each side: hips turn first, racket last
steps.why: Your arm fires first. Hip Snaps install ground → hips → trunk → arm so the racket head is the fastest link, which fixes balls flying long or into the net.

steps.dose: 3 shadow swings each at low / waist / high contact, then 6 lateral shuffles, stick 1 s, swing
steps.why: Reference swings calibrate contact height; sticking each set-up position replaces reaching and lunging with moving the feet first.

steps.dose: 1 min mini-tennis, 2 min baseline at 70 → 90%
steps.why: Gradual ramp maps the installed pattern onto real balls before points count.

anchorCue: Between points: split-step bounce, eyes on the opponent's strings.
airwayNote: Tennis is intermittent high intensity, which suits an interval-style warm-up: the split-step pogos and rally ramp provide it (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Short bursts to HR ~165-180. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Long static shoulder or hamstring stretches before
Max-effort serves in the first 3 minutes
Changing grip or technique on match day
teachMe: A groundstroke is a rotation transfer from the floor to the racket. Each body segment accelerates and then brakes so the next one goes faster. If the arm starts it, contact gets random because the arm is doing a job the hips should do. Installing hip-first now means you don't have to think about it during the match.

steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Pickleball punishes tension: a gripping body pops the ball up. The exhale releases the brake; the isometric wakes up recruitment for fast hands.

steps.dose: 10 soft tosses toward your face that you block with a still paddle, then 20 s near-far (paddle face → far baseline)
steps.why: Hands battles at the kitchen trigger the flinch. Blocking easy balls teaches the brain an incoming ball is safe, which speeds up reactions.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, then hold ready position 60 s (knees ~25°, hip hinge ~15°, paddle up, weight slightly forward)
steps.why: Holding the exact ready angles for 60 s installs the position so you default to it instead of standing tall and reaching.

steps.dose: 3 shadow strokes each at low (dink), chest (block), overhead; then 6 side shuffles to a dink, stick 1 s
steps.why: Reference strokes calibrate paddle angle per height. Sticking each shuffle installs feet-first instead of lunging.

steps.dose: 6 Hip Snaps, then 6 shadow drives with hips leading
steps.why: Drives and overheads go long when the arm leads. Hip-first turns the paddle into the end of a whip.

steps.dose: 1 min dinks, 1 min drives at 70 → 90%
steps.why: Puts real balls on the installed pattern before points count.

anchorCue: Between points: paddle up, sit into ready.
avoid: Static stretching before
Smashing at 100% in the first minute
teachMe: At the kitchen, the winner is usually whoever is already in position. Ready position puts your center of mass over a wide, arched base so the first move needs no wind-up. Eyes that aren't afraid of the ball pick up the opponent's paddle angle earlier, which buys you time you don't feel but you'll see.

steps.drill: Box breathing + wall push isometric (acceleration lean)
steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push in a 45° sprint lean, one knee driven up
steps.why: The lean isometric rehearses the exact acceleration angle and recruits more high-threshold units.

steps.dose: 20 s near-far, then pick one point at the finish and lock eyes on it for 3 breaths
steps.why: A steady gaze keeps the head still, which keeps the trunk still, which keeps force going straight back into the track.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 20 pogos, 2 × 15 m A-skips
steps.why: Sprinting is elastic: short ground contacts depend on a stiff Achilles and an arch that doesn't collapse. Pogos tune that spring right before you need it.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 wall-drill switches, 3 falling starts into 10 m
steps.why: Grooves the push-back-and-down force direction of acceleration so the first three steps aren't wasted upward.

steps.dose: 3 × 30-40 m at 70/85/95%, full walk-back rest
steps.why: Ramps the nervous system to race speed and acts as an interval warm-up for the airways.

anchorCue: In the blocks or stance: push the ground away.
airwayNote: Short sprints are less of an EIB trigger than long runs, but the warm-up still matters: interval/variable-intensity warm-ups reduced post-exercise lung-function drop (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B), protection roughly 1-2 h. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Static stretching before
Max sprints before a full warm-up
Heavy lifting earlier the same day
teachMe: Sprint speed = how much force you can put into the ground during a very short contact, and in which direction. A flat foot lengthens contact time because the arch has to sag before it can push. The pogos and Screw shorten that window so more of each contact becomes forward propulsion.

steps.dose: 3 breaths, then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Lowers threat arousal so passing arms stay quiet instead of swinging at the ball.

steps.dose: 10 tosses toward your chest received on still forearms
steps.why: Watching the ball onto a still platform kills the flinch that sends passes everywhere.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 15 pogos, 30 s ready position (knees ~25°, hips ~15°, weight forward)
steps.why: Sets an arched, stiff base so the first move to the ball is instant.

steps.drill: Approach Step-and-Stick + Hip Snap arm swing
steps.dose: 4 approaches landing two-footed and freezing 1 s, then 6 standing arm swings where the hips open before the arm
steps.why: Freezing the landing installs safe knee alignment for flat feet; hip-first arm swings make hits harder and less random.

steps.dose: 3 approach jumps at 70/85/95%, then 5 hits at 80%
steps.why: Ramps elastic loading and the hitting chain before game speed.

anchorCue: Before the serve: bounce once, land in ready.
avoid: Static stretching before
Max jumps or full-speed spikes in the first minutes
teachMe: A spike is a vertical jump plus a whip. The jump depends on an elastic, stiff base, and the hit depends on the order the segments fire. Get the foot and the order right before the first point, so the game just runs the pattern.

steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push in fight stance
steps.why: Threat state shows up as freezing under strikes. A long, controlled breath tells the nervous system the situation is safe enough to see clearly; the isometric primes full recruitment.

steps.dose: 10 slow glove/hand pushes toward your face that you watch and parry (sibling or wall), then 20 s soft-focus on the chest while noticing hands at the edges
steps.why: Eyes closing or turning away on incoming strikes is the core fear response. Slow, safe approaches recalibrate it before contact.

steps.drill: The Screw in stance + level-change pogos
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw in stance, 2 × 10 pogos into a sprawl-ready level change
steps.why: A rooted, arched stance stops the knee caving and lets force travel from the floor into punches and shots.

steps.drill: Hip Snap → jab-cross shadow + Step-and-Stick level change
steps.dose: 6 Hip Snaps, 1 round (60 s) shadow jab-cross with hips leading, 4 penetration steps freezing 1 s at the bottom
steps.why: Installs ground → hips → shoulder → fist and a balanced shot entry, so your arm stops punching alone.

steps.dose: 2 × 30 s at 70% → 90% (mitts with sibling at contact-ladder level 1, or shadow), 2 sprawls
steps.why: Ramps intensity without fatigue. At home with your younger sibling stay on contact-ladder levels 0-2: shadow, pads, cooperative drilling.

anchorCue: Between exchanges: exhale through the nose, chin down, tripod feet.
airwayNote: Rounds are interval efforts, so the ramp above doubles as a variable-intensity airway warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Bursts to HR ~170-190, recover between. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Hard sparring as a warm-up
Static stretching before
Learning a brand-new technique right before live rounds
Above contact-ladder level 2 with your younger sibling
teachMe: Power in a strike is not arm strength: it's how fast and in what order you transfer force from the floor. Each link speeds up then brakes to fling the next. Fear narrows vision and makes you grip, which slows every link. Calm eyes plus a rooted foot is the fastest path to a harder, cleaner punch.

steps.drill: Downshift breathing + wall push isometric (shot angle)
steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push in a low penetration-step angle
steps.why: Rehearses the drive angle at max intent and calms the gripping response that makes you stiff in ties.

steps.dose: 30 s: eyes soft on a partner's (or imagined) hips while tracking hand movement in peripheral vision
steps.why: Hips don't fake; watching them with a wide field lets you react to level changes earlier.

steps.drill: The Screw in stance + level-change pogos
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw in stance, 2 × 10 small hops dropping into stance on landing
steps.why: Sets an arched foot and stiff ankles so the shot leaves from the floor instead of from bent-over arms.

steps.dose: 6 penetration steps freezing 1 s at the bottom, 6 hip escapes (shrimps) each way
steps.why: Freezing at the bottom installs head-up, hips-under alignment; shrimps groove the escape pattern with no thought needed.

steps.dose: 3 shots at 70/85/95% speed, 3 sprawls
steps.why: Ramps to match speed and doubles as an interval warm-up. With your younger sibling stay on contact-ladder levels 0-2.

anchorCue: Reset in stance: tripod feet, hips under.
airwayNote: Wrestling is anaerobic intervals with hard breathing, an EIB trigger. The shot/sprawl ramp is your variable-intensity warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Bursts to HR ~175-190. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Live goes as a warm-up
Static stretching before
Neck bridges at max load before matches
teachMe: A takedown wins at the floor: the drive comes from feet pushing back so the hips go forward. A collapsing arch angles that push sideways. Lock the base, then rehearse the shape at full speed once, so the match just replays it.

steps.drill: Box breathing + wall push isometric in stance
steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push from your boxing stance (rear hand)
steps.why: A long exhale turns off the flinch/freeze reflex; the max isometric from stance primes the exact chain you'll punch with.

steps.dose: 10 slow glove/hand pushes toward your face (sibling or wall partner) that you watch until the last moment and parry, then 6 slow slips keeping eyes open
steps.why: Blinking or looking away on punches is the threat response. Slow, safe approaches teach the brain to keep the eyes open, which is the start of all defense.

steps.drill: The Screw in stance + pogos in stance
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 15 small bounce pogos in stance
steps.why: Arched feet and a springy ankle let you push off for footwork and drive the ground into the punch.

steps.drill: Hip Snap → jab-cross shadow with Step-and-Stick
steps.dose: 6 Hip Snaps, then 1 round (90 s) shadow: step in, jab-cross, stick 1 s balanced, step out
steps.why: Installs ground → hips → shoulder → fist; the 1 s freeze makes sure you finish every combo on balance instead of falling in.

steps.dose: 2 × 45 s at 70% → 90% (pads with sibling at contact-ladder level 1, or shadow)
steps.why: Ramps speed and heart rate without fatigue. At home with your younger sibling: contact-ladder levels 0-2 only.

anchorCue: Between rounds: long exhale, chin down, bounce.
airwayNote: Rounds are interval efforts; this ramp doubles as a variable-intensity airway warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Bursts to HR ~170-190, recover between. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Hard sparring as a warm-up
Static stretches before
Max-power bag work before technique
Above contact-ladder level 2 with your younger sibling
teachMe: A cross is a chain: the back foot pushes the floor, the hip turns, the trunk turns, the shoulder fires and the fist lands last. Each link has to brake to hand speed to the next one. If the arm starts first, the big engines never contribute. Calm eyes give you the time to throw it right.

steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s max-intent bridge press against the floor
steps.why: BJJ rewards calm. A long exhale prevents the panic-grip that burns your arms out in the first roll.

steps.dose: 20 s soft gaze noticing the whole room, then 20 s eyes closed doing slow shrimps
steps.why: Grappling relies on feel as much as sight; eyes-closed movement sharpens body position sense (proprioception).

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 6 bridges, 6 shrimps each side
steps.why: Hip-driven movement starts from the feet. Setting the foot tripod makes bridges and escapes powerful instead of arm-pushes.

steps.dose: 4 technical stand-ups each side, 4 hip escapes freezing 1 s on the frame
steps.why: Freezing at the end of each escape installs the frame-then-hip order.

steps.dose: 2 × 60 s at 50% → 80% (cooperative; with sibling stay at contact-ladder levels 0-2)
steps.why: Gradually loads grip and breathing before live rounds.

airwayNote: Long rolls can trigger EIB. The flow-roll ramp is a variable-intensity warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Max-effort rolls as a warm-up
Neck cranks or heavy neck bridges before rolling
Above contact-ladder level 2 with your younger sibling; tap early
teachMe: In grappling, the panicked body grips everything and tires in minutes. Exhaling resets the threat signal so you can feel pressure and move your hips instead of pushing with arms. Hips win; arms only frame.

steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Lowers tension so the wrist and forearm stay loose for touch.

steps.dose: 20 s saccades, 20 s pursuit of a moving ball, 20 s near-far
steps.why: Table tennis has the shortest reaction windows of your sports. Fast eyes buy milliseconds you can't get anywhere else.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, hold ready position 45 s (knees ~25°, hips ~15°, weight forward)
steps.why: A low, arched base lets you shift weight side to side without standing up.

steps.drill: Hip Snap → shadow forehand + Three Contact Points
steps.dose: 6 Hip Snaps, 10 shadow forehands with hips turning first, 3 shadows each at low / middle / high
steps.why: Even small strokes start from the hips. Installing this order stops arm-only flicks that fly long.

steps.dose: 1 min controlled rally, 1 min at game speed
steps.why: Maps the pattern onto real balls before the score counts.

avoid: Static stretching before
Smashing at 100% before you've rallied
teachMe: In table tennis, vision and timing are almost everything. Priming the eyes and a stable, low base lets you see spin earlier and hit with the body instead of chasing with the arm.

steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 3 min easy jog nasal-breathing only (HR ~120-140)
steps.why: Controlled breathing lowers pre-race nerves; nasal-only pace keeps the start easy on the airways.

steps.dose: 30 s looking ~20 m ahead at a steady point; mentally run the first 400 m
steps.why: Steady gaze keeps the head and trunk quiet, which saves energy every stride.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 20 pogos, 2 × 15 m A-skips
steps.why: Your flat feet sag on each step, wasting energy. Pogos stiffen the Achilles spring so more of each landing comes back as push-off.

steps.drill: Cadence strides to music or count
steps.dose: 2 × 20 s at goal race pace, targeting 170-180 steps/min
steps.why: Higher cadence shortens ground contact and reduces overstriding; locking it in now means you don't have to count during the race.

steps.dose: 4 × 30 s fast (HR ~170-185) / 30 s walk, finish 10-15 min before the gun
steps.why: Interval/variable-intensity warm-ups reduced exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (Stickland 2012 systematic review), which matters for your post-run wheezing.

anchorCue: When it hurts: 'quick feet, strong arms.'
airwayNote: This is your highest-risk sport for EIB. The 4 × 30 s interval block is the airway warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B). Many people get a protective 'refractory' window of roughly 1-2 h, some up to ~2-4 h, and about half of asthmatics respond (Mickleborough 2007). Finish it ~10-15 min before the start. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up. Your baseline: ~8:22/mile at ~173 avg HR; max HR ~200-205.
avoid: Long static stretching
Going out faster than your goal pace in the first 400 m
New shoes or a new breakfast on race day
teachMe: Running economy is how much oxygen each step costs. Stiff, springy ankles return energy; collapsing arches absorb it. The pogos and Screw tune the spring, cadence keeps contacts short, and the interval warm-up protects your airways so you can actually breathe at race pace.

steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: New sports trigger threat (unfamiliar = unsafe to the brain). Slow exhales lower it so you can learn instead of freezing.

steps.dose: 20 s saccades, 20 s near-far, 10 tosses toward you that you catch
steps.why: Opens up vision before you need it and reduces flinch to a moving object.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 20 s single-leg tripod balance each side, 2 × 15 pogos
steps.why: Universal base for any sport: arched foot, aligned knee, stiff ankle.

steps.drill: Hip Snap drill + slow-motion sport movement
steps.dose: 6 Hip Snaps, then 6 slow-motion reps of the sport's main move (golf swing, throw, stroke) with hips leading
steps.why: Almost every hitting or throwing sport uses ground → hips → trunk → arm. Slow reps of the new move with that order give the brain a clean first map.

steps.drill: Speed ramp of the main move
steps.dose: 3 reps each at 50 / 70 / 90% speed
steps.why: Brings the new pattern up to speed gradually so it holds under real tempo.

anchorCue: Before each rep: tripod feet, hips start it.
avoid: Static stretching before
Swinging at 100% on the first try
Overloading on tips: pick one install, then play
teachMe: The first session in a new sport writes the brain's first draft of the movement. If that draft is arm-first and fearful, it's harder to rewrite later. A calm, hip-first, rooted first draft is the shortcut to looking like you've played before.
